title: What did North, South, East & West originally mean?

entries.note: Literally a description of the earth, from geo- meaning earth plus -graphy, the process of writing, recording or drawing.
Used in Greek and Latin for the ends of an axis, originally the axis of the rotating night sky; the magnetic sense came later.
Literally a glob; it only came to mean planet Earth in the mid-1500s, shortly before the [[see:Globe Theatre]] was named.
Named not long after [[see:globe]] came to mean planet Earth.
Essentially meant ground before it meant the planet, like Latin [[see:terra]].
Offered as a parallel to [[see:earth]] meaning ground before planet.
So called because it divides the earth into equal parts, two equal halves.
From Greek [[from:tropos]], turn, after the sun appearing to turn back at the solstice; related to [[same-root:trope]] and [[same-root:zoetrope]].
The northern tropic at about 23.4 degrees, where the sun appears to turn back at the June solstice; used to explain [[see:tropics]].
The other tropic, named alongside the [[see:Tropic of Cancer]] in explaining the sun's apparent reversal.
Related to [[same-root:tropics]]; a figurative turn, direction or recurring element in storytelling, probably via Latin [[from:tropus]], a turn of phrase.
An early spinning moving-picture device, often showing a galloping horse; the name meant movement spin, related to [[same-root:tropics]].
Latin for a figure of speech, literally a turn of phrase, probably where the storytelling sense of [[gave:trope]] comes from.
The north-to-south lines, which are longer; remembered with the mnemonic "long is tall and lat is fat", contrasting with [[see:latitude]].
The shorter lines across the globe, remembered as "lat is fat" in contrast with [[see:longitude]].
Literally the same as [[same-root:container]]: con, together, plus a root meaning held, so areas held together; related to [[same-root:incontinence]].
Given as literally the same word as [[same-root:continent]].
Being unable to contain yourself; originally unrestrained sexual desire, later inability to contain one's bowels; related to [[same-root:continent]].
From Latin [[from:contra]], that which is opposite you: the land you look out upon and are confronted with.
Reflects the earlier notion of [[see:country]] as the land in front of you.
Borrowed by painters from Dutch [[from:landschap]], literally land-ship, meaning a painting of countryside before it meant the scenery itself.
Suffix in [[see:lordship]] and [[see:friendship]], also at the end of [[see:landscape]]; means shaped like or shaping, related to [[same-root:shape]] and German [[same-root:-schaft]].
Example of the suffix [[see:-ship]].
Example of the suffix [[see:-ship]].
Related to the suffix [[same-root:-ship]] and the -scape of [[see:landscape]].
German suffix meaning the same thing as English [[same-root:-ship]].
Contains [[see:deer]]: Old English [[from:wilddeor]], wild animals, plus Middle English -ness; a place of wild beasts, later glossed as a [[see:desert]].
Originally a general word for a beast or animal, later narrowed; Old English used [[see:heorot]] and [[see:dā]] for deer.
One of the Old English words for [[see:deer]], today's hart; also the name of the hall [[see:Heorot]].
Old English word for a female [[see:deer]], today's doe.
The hall in Beowulf, named for the stag ([[from:heorot]]) because royalty was associated with stags.
Essentially a noun form of Greek [[from:bios]], life: a place where life is.
Rob's first association with [[see:biome]], such as gut bacteria; simply a small biome.

Something rising above the earth, related to [[same-root:mount]], [[same-root:eminent]], [[same-root:menace]], [[same-root:promontory]] and [[same-root:prominent]]; no firm size distinction from [[see:hill]].
Related to [[same-root:mountain]], and etymologically basically the same word as [[same-root:mound]].
Related to [[same-root:mountain]], sharing its sticking-out sense.
Related to [[same-root:mountain]], sharing its sticking-out sense.
Related to [[same-root:mountain]]; the hosts debate its pronunciation and confirm the stress falls on the first syllable.
Also related to [[same-root:mountain]].
Etymologically basically the same word as [[same-root:mount]].
No agreed distinction from [[see:mountain]]: definitions vary by country and surrounding terrain; hill is Germanic, mountain Romance.
Australian peak called the world's smallest [[see:mountain]], only 141 feet (43 m) tall; Jess is unsure of its pronunciation.
Via French, short for Latin [[from:forestis silva]], outside woods: royal hunting grounds set apart, not necessarily wooded; related to [[same-root:foreign]].
The Germanic equivalent of Romance [[see:forest]].
Related to Latin silva, the wood part of the phrase behind [[see:forest]].
Related to [[same-root:forest]] through the Latin for outside; used for an outsider.
Unlike a [[see:forest]], by definition has trees; woodland words had a whole episode in an earlier season.
A modern term first found in early-1900s ecological literature, now the preferred scientific term for the biome once called [[see:jungle]].
From Hindi, meaning any wilderness or uncultivated land, from a Sanskrit word for arid terrain; English speakers applied it to dense forest, now [[see:rainforest]].
Means a place deserted of people, not a sandy place; from Latin [[from:deserere]], to unjoin, related to [[same-root:series]]; equated with [[see:wilderness]].
Meant an island that is deserted, not a sandy island, as the hosts point out about [[see:desert]].
Related to the -serere of the Latin behind [[same-root:desert]]: to desert is to take something out of a series.
Means desert, so "Sahara desert" means desert desert, a [[see:pleonasm]] that doesn't sound wrong because Sahara is also a name.
Redundant repetition, used mostly in linguistics; unlike a [[see:tautology]], it doesn't sound wrong, as with [[see:Sahara]] desert.
Close to [[see:pleonasm]] but also used in maths and elsewhere, and tends to sound more wrong, as with [[see:ATM machine]].
Example of a [[see:tautology]] that sounds repetitive if you know what ATM stands for.
There are many; Avon is from the old Celtic word for river, so the name means river river.
England has several; Ouse was the Viking word for a river, making the name another tautology.
From an Ojibwe term meaning great river, so it means great river river.
Its name means lake lake.
Mauna means mountain, so "Mount Mauna Kea" repeats itself; the world's tallest mountain from base to tip, though lower in elevation than [[see:Everest]].
Climbing [[see:Mauna Kea]] from base to top would mean ascending farther than on Everest.
From Spanish [[from:sabana]], treeless plain, from Taíno [[from:zabana]]: a Caribbean word later applied to an African biome; compare [[see:steppe]].
An indigenous African name meaning endless plain in the Maa language of the Maasai.
From Russian, meaning a treeless plain like [[see:savannah]]; a Russian word because the steppes lie mostly around Russia.
A French word for North America's grasslands, since the French were there to name them; similar in meaning to [[see:steppe]].
Russian word for boreal forest, possibly of Turkic or Mongolic origin; the largest terrestrial biome, with conifers, permafrost and fires.
Means northern, as in [[see:aurora borealis]]; used to describe the [[see:taiga]].
The northern lights; borealis is a later Latin term for northern, unlike classical [[see:septentriones]].
Essentially means something squidgy; directly related to German [[same-root:Schwamm]] and to [[same-root:sump]].
Directly related to [[same-root:swamp]]; can mean a mushroom or a sponge.
Makeup sponge used on Rob in TV makeup, a little [[see:Schwamm]], so he was dabbed with a mini [[see:swamp]].
Related to [[same-root:swamp]]; recorded since the mid-1500s, originally meaning a marsh, with the water-collecting pit sense from around 1650.
An Old English word for a wetland, one of many English wetland words.
An Irish word for a wetland; ecologically a rain-fed acidic wetland with slow decomposition, often peat, which preserves [[see:bog bodies]].
Pulled out of peat bogs because the conditions of a [[see:bog]] preserve them well.
An Old English word for marsh.
Described as an Old Norse word for a marsh.
The most recent wetland word, an 18th-century compound of the older words wet and land.
From Latin [[from:riparia]], riverbank, while [[see:fluvius]] and [[see:amnis]] described the water; named for the bank, not the water.
A Latin word for the river water itself, unlike the bank word behind [[see:river]].
Another Latin word for the river water itself, contrasted with the bank word behind [[see:river]].
Pertains to rivers and streams, originally to riverbanks in Latin; related to [[same-root:river]].
One of two French words for river alongside [[see:fleuve]]; hard to distinguish, perhaps by size; reflects the bank origin of [[same-root:river]].
French word for river alongside [[see:rivière]]; Rob thinks one is bigger than the other.
The left bank of the Seine in Paris; rive is related to the Latin bank word behind [[same-root:river]].
From Latin [[from:lacus]], basin or reservoir: named for the space holding the water, not the water.
A Germanic, Old English word related to [[same-root:pound]] as in impound: the enclosure where the water lives.
In the sense of impound, related to [[same-root:pond]].
Properly an enclosed area of water rather than the [[see:ocean]]; Britons say sea where Americans say ocean; compare German [[see:See]].
German word that can mean a sea, as in Nordsee, the North Sea, or simply a lake.
From Latin [[from:Oceanus]], borrowed from Greek [[from:Okeanos]], the world-encircling river and its god.
In early Greek cosmology the river ringing the flat disc of the world, source of rivers, clouds and rain, and its god; gave [[gave:ocean]].
Has an ancient root meaning left, because people orientated themselves facing the rising sun in the east.
Shares a root with [[same-root:sun]], since in the northern hemisphere the sun is always to the south.
Shares a root with [[same-root:south]].
From an ancient root meaning to become light, where the sun rises; related to [[same-root:ushas]], [[same-root:aurora]] and [[same-root:australis]]; unusual among Germanic ost-forms.
Sanskrit for the dawn, related to [[same-root:east]].
Related to [[same-root:east]].
Means southern though related to [[same-root:east]]; possibly because Romans misjudged the angle of the Italian peninsula, confusing east and south.
Named by Jess as linked to [[see:australis]].
Named as linked to [[see:australis]], meaning southern.
Has an ancient root meaning evening, where the sun sets; a cognate of Latin [[same-root:vesper]], not from it.
Latin for evening, related to [[same-root:west]].
Irish and Scottish Gaelic word meaning both westward and behind you, from facing the rising sun; unrelated to [[see:west]].
Like the other French compass points, borrowed from English [[from:north]], then passed on to Spanish.
French compass point borrowed from English [[from:south]], later passed into Spanish.
French compass point borrowed from English [[from:west]], later passed into Spanish.
French compass point borrowed from English [[from:east]], later passed into Spanish.
Jess's other example of a basic word going from English into French, though much later than [[see:nord]] and the other compass points.
The classical Latin word for north, referring to [[see:Ursa Major]], the Plough, which points to the North Star.
The constellation called the Plough in Britain and the Big Dipper elsewhere, referred to by [[see:septentriones]].
Means with bears, after a constellation, contrasting with [[see:Antarctic]]; neatly, polar bears live only in the north; discussed before on the show.
Means without bears, the opposite of [[see:Arctic]]; fittingly there are no polar bears at the South Pole.
From the Latin for east, paired with [[see:occident]]; as a verb it was back-formed from [[see:orientate]].
From the Latin for the west, the counterpart of [[see:orient]].
Being unable to tell where you are, literally not knowing which way east is; preferred in America over British [[see:disorientated]].
The British form; to disorientate is to undo having found east, whereas to disorient is never having found it—a minute difference from [[see:disoriented]].
A [[see:back-formation]] from orientation; the verb [[gave:orient]] was then back-formed again.
Back-formations tend to be seen as lesser than original words, a mark against [[see:disorientated]], which Rob will keep saying anyway.
